metadata.title: Building Skills for All in Australia (EN)

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: This OECD report uses the Survey of Adult Skills (PIAAC) microdata for Australia, drawing on two rounds of data collection (2011-2012 and 2014-2015) and reporting results for literacy and numeracy (and separately PSTRE in another chapter). The report describes how “low skills” are defined using PIAAC proficiency levels (below Level 2) and how proficiency scales are interpreted (0–500 points with levels). However, the excerpt provided does not specify whether analysts applied PIAAC sampling weights or replicate weights (e.g., BRR/jackknife) in the reported comparisons. For users replicating or extending the analyses with PIAAC public data, the appropriate approach is to apply the complex survey design weights supplied with the PIAAC database when estimating population-representative statistics; PV handling is typically required for cognitive achievement scales, but this report primarily presents level-based and descriptive/policy comparisons rather than a documented PV/ML estimation pipeline.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: The report is a policy analysis and descriptive synthesis of PIAAC results (e.g., shares below proficiency thresholds, adjusted differences from regression models) rather than an empirical machine-learning study with a documented plausible-values (PV) estimation procedure. Because the excerpt does not provide a PV estimation method (e.g., Rubin’s rules across PVs) or a missing-data strategy for an achievement-score modeling pipeline, the PV and missing-data handling details are not available from the provided text. This is therefore treated as a reporting gap for methodological transparency rather than evidence that PVs/missingness were not relevant to the underlying PIAAC analyses.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: The report focuses on Australia and defines low skills using PIAAC literacy and numeracy proficiency levels (below Level 2). It reports that the Survey of Adult Skills was conducted in Australia from October 2011 to March 2012 with a total of 7 430 adults aged 16-65. The excerpt does not specify additional analytic exclusions (e.g., computer-based assessment opt-out handling for PSTRE, missing background-item exclusions, or any restriction to particular subpopulations within Australia), so the filtering criteria are limited to the low-skill definition and the Australia sample described.

data.outcome_summary: This OECD report uses the Survey of Adult Skills (PIAAC) to characterize low-skilled adults in Australia and to discuss policy-relevant correlates and consequences of low literacy and numeracy (with PSTRE treated separately in another chapter). It defines “low skills” as adults below Level 2 in literacy or numeracy and reports population shares and subgroup patterns (e.g., age, gender, migrant status, parental education) alongside labour-market and well-being associations. The report also highlights system strengths (e.g., ICT-related skills and workplace learning opportunities) and challenges (notably numeracy performance and gender gaps in numeracy/STEM pathways). While the text mentions adjusted differences based on regression models for some well-being outcomes, it does not provide an explicit machine-learning modeling pipeline, PV-combining rules, or a documented missing-data strategy in the excerpt. Consequently, the contribution is primarily policy interpretation of PIAAC proficiency distributions and related outcomes rather than ML-based predictive results.
